Furthermore, there are three kinds of cultivation: namely, guarding, practicing, and refining; therefore, nothing is lacking.
Moreover, the Path may also be said to be a mental dharma. Why is this?
Because it arises and ceases simultaneously with right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), it is like a single mind.
As the Sūtra says:
"By making the mind predominant, one attains a single mind; this is called mental concentration (*citta-samādhi*), which is a factor of the Path."
Because they share the same renunciation and accomplish the same purpose, they are united in a single mind and do not conflict with one another.
As for your question: if the Path reaches the removal of afflictions, then mutually contradictory factors would exist simultaneously within a single mind;
if it does not reach them, why would they not be removed in the mental continuum of another?
Answer:
The Path does not reach the defilements, yet it is able to eliminate them.

Just as the Path does not reach the breaking of precepts, yet it can eliminate one's own breaking of precepts without eliminating another's breaking of precepts, so too is the elimination of defilements.
Although it does not reach either one's own or another's continuum, it can only eliminate one's own afflictions and cannot eliminate those of others.
The Vibhajyavādins say:
"It neither reaches nor does not reach; at this time, afflictions are eliminated because non-arising constitutes cessation."
For example, when treating a disease, once the sensation of suffering has already arisen, the physician can no longer treat it. Why is this?
Because it is impossible to transform suffering into pleasure.
If painful sensation has not yet arrived, even a physician does not treat it.
Why is this? Because it does not exist.
If that is so, what is it that is counteracted?
It merely acts as an adverse condition, ensuring that suffering which has not yet arisen never arises.
The Path’s ability to eliminate delusion is likewise the same.
Regarding your question: "If they arise simultaneously, there would be multiple acts of attention (*manasikāra*); if they arise sequentially, there would be only one part," the answer is:

They may arise simultaneously because they accomplish a single purpose; it is not because they take different objects that there is no simultaneous arising of multiple mental states. Their differentiation is visible through their functional capacities, just as in the case of desire (*chanda*) and so forth.
Regarding your question, "Why are exactly eight factors established, neither more nor less?
the answer is:
this question is inexhaustible; therefore, I set it aside without answering.
Furthermore, the eight factors are taught because they serve as the antidotes to the eightfold wrong path.
Furthermore, they are taught for the purpose of encompassing the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Furthermore, the eight factors are taught as the antidotes to the three thorns, the three fetters, the three fires, and the three poisons.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: Because it can accomplish a mind endowed with eight qualities, it is called the "eightfold [path].

Through the attainment of right view, the mind becomes pure; through the attainment of right resolve, the mind becomes fresh and clean; through the attainment of right speech, the mind becomes balanced and even; through the attainment of right action, the mind becomes free from remorse; through the attainment of right livelihood, the mind becomes supple and smooth; through the attainment of right effort, the mind follows the teaching; through the attainment of right mindfulness, the mind becomes settled; and through the attainment of right concentration, the mind becomes immovable.
Regarding your question as to why [the sūtra] does not mention other factors such as desire (*chanda*) and so forth:

the answer is that it mentions only the superior factors; or those that are powerful in function; or those capable of bearing the heavy burden; or those that collectively encompass right speech, right action, and right livelihood, which are the factors conducive to stream-entry (*srotāpatti-aṅga*). This is because faith (*śraddhā*) subsumes these three.
The stream-enterer (srotāpanna) possesses the fourfold wisdom and faith; desire itself is this faith.
Furthermore, this faith is also subsumed under right view, because the person who is a stream-enterer has attained wisdom and faith.
Joy, tranquility, equanimity, and right concentration are included [within the factors].
Therefore, these eight factors encompass all [the factors] exhaustively.
As for your question: how is it that one dharma is explained in three ways; or how is it said that the Middle Way can extinguish both merit and evil, leading to the end of suffering?
Answer:
It is due to three superior functions.

For example, the sun is called "light" because it can dispel darkness; it is called "day" because it can distinguish day from night; and it is called the "basis of time" because it can distinguish moments (*kṣaṇa*) and so forth.

The Noble Path is likewise: because it can distance one from the two extremes, it is called the Middle Way; because it can eliminate both black and white karma, it is called the extinction of merit and evil; and because it uproots the suffering of body and mind, it is said that practicing this path leads to the end of suffering.
Alternatively, because the paths of the three periods of time are excluded, it is said that "practice leads to the exhaustion of suffering.
As for your question, "Why is right view said to be the first? the answer is as follows:
Because it serves as the foremost, it is likened to a king; as the Sūtra says:
"Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), Prajñā is the most supreme.

Furthermore, because it can produce superior merit: if wisdom is supreme, all virtues are likewise supreme. For example, because of his right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), Śāriputra did not look at the faces of others; because of his right view, the householder Śūra’s mind was difficult to move; because of this right view, King Aśoka could not be led astray by others; and because the householder Citta was able to uproot the very source of calamities and misfortunes.
As the Sūtra says:
"Because of the arising of clear knowledge (*vidyā*), ignorance (*avidyā*) is extinguished.
Therefore, right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is the first [member].
To your question, "How is one described as having previously practiced?
the answer is:
By attaining right view, the remaining factors attain the supramundane, the untainted, and the unshared.
Or it is said that by the power of right view, the remaining factors obtain the name of the path of liberation,
as the Sūtra says:
"O Bhikṣus!"
This person of right view performs actions of body, speech, and mind so as to obtain desirable and excellent fruits, as explained at length in the sūtras;
therefore, they take right view as their precursor.
Regarding your question, "What is the meaning of right view?
the answer is:
View is defined as non-erroneous realization and illumination; it is the non-erroneous realization and illumination of the true nature upon which one relies.
Furthermore, *tathatā* (suchness) means "correct," and "contemplation" means "vision"; because one contemplates the noble truths as they truly are, it is called "right view.
Furthermore, "correct" has the sense of being praiseworthy, and "vision" has the sense of light; because it is a praiseworthy light, it is called "right view."
As the Sūtra says:
"Among all lights, this light is the most supreme; that is to say, right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, the knowledge, object, and practice of supreme virtue are called right view."
Why is this? Because this stage of right determination is designated as "right view," as stated in the *Bījopama-sūtra*.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
Because the object is correct, cognition is correct; it is not because cognition is correct that the object is correct.
Since they are associated with the characteristics of the conditioned and the outflows, all things are exclusively suffering.
To know this with certainty is called right view, as the Buddha taught to Mahākātyāyana.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"That wisdom which counteracts ignorance, doubt regarding wisdom, and inverted wisdom, and which is able to transcend suffering and so forth—this true wisdom is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)."
Regarding your question: since the "seer" does not exist, who is it that sees?
Answer:
This seeing is accomplished through the gathering of various conditions; there is no separate, singular entity that acts as the seer, just as in the case of flowers and fruits.
Furthermore, as a verse says:
"There is seeing, yet there is no seer; what dharma is the seer?
Arising from the conjunction of conditions, the claim that 'it sees form' is false."
This dharma is seen at the time of its aggregation; when combined and dispersed, it cannot be seen.
It is produced solely through causes and conditions, like a person with distorted limbs who lacks [normal] function.
Dharmas arise from conditions and cannot be said to belong to a single [entity]. As the Buddha taught in order to refute the *guṇas*:
I do not say that consciousness is that which cognizes. Why?
Because this is established as a complete conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
Regarding your question as to how right view differs from the right view within the ten wholesome paths of action:
the answer is that conventional wisdom resides in the ten wholesome paths, while true wisdom resides in the eightfold noble path.
That which can induce future births, taking suffering as its fruit and observing karma as its object—such right view resides within the ten wholesome dharmas.
That which can extinguish the three realms of existence, taking nirvana as its fruit and taking the Truths as its object—such right view resides within the Eightfold Noble Path.
Regarding your question: "If one perceives the truths all at once by means of right view, there would have to be multiple objects;
if this were not the case, then [the mind] would not be subject to momentary destruction.
Answer:
Because one can accomplish four matters simultaneously, it is said to occur "at once"; this is not because the objects differ.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"The practitioner cultivating contemplation penetrates the pores with noble wisdom and is able to sever all afflictions."
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"If one comprehensively contemplates the three types of sensation, all that is to be done has been accomplished, and there is nothing further to be performed.
Because one does so through the common characteristics of the dharmas—the truth of suffering and the characteristic of non-self—one simultaneously comprehensively contemplates the four truths."
As in the sequential contemplation, the objects of impermanence, suffering, and non-self simultaneously encompass the Truth of Suffering.
Regarding your question: "If one has already fully realized all the Truths through right view, what further use is there for the remaining portions?"
Answer:
All the constituent parts are capable of extinguishing their respective opposites, each having its own specific function, just as in the case of inducing vomiting followed by purging.
Furthermore, regarding all these constituent parts:
Each acts as a leader within its own respective function, yet together they accomplish a single task.
This is like the parts of a chariot:
each has its own specific function, yet together they accomplish the act of transport.
The same applies to the factors of the path and the path itself.
As for your question regarding the meaning of "perfectly awakened" (samyaksambuddha): [it refers to one who has fully realized the truth].
Answer: It is unprecedented that today he is reckoned as being born;
this is called Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Furthermore, this is the Dharma of equality, because it arises through the conditions of perception and mental formations (*saṃjñā-saṃskāra-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, because the essence, characteristics, objects, and fruits mutually support and harmonize one another, it is called Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Furthermore, as in the case of seeing and subsequently discerning without abandoning [the object], it is called Perfect Enlightenment, like the rumination of a cow.
Regarding your question, "How do three dharmas become one?
the answer is:
because they share the same characteristic, just as in the case of the other factors of the path.
Furthermore, listen well: because they are reckoned as equal, they are like the factors of concentration (*samādhi-aṅga*).
Furthermore, because they take nirvāṇa as their object, they are like the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*); thus, the three become one.

Regarding your question: "If one realizes the exhaustion of outflows by relying on the two higher absorptions (dhyānas), then perfect enlightenment would not be possessed and there would be a deficiency in the factors of the path; this point must be resolved. Answer:

If one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path by relying on the two higher absorptions, it is simply that the factors of initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) belonging to the first absorption are absent; it is not that the factor of enlightenment within the factors of the path is absent. This is, for example, like how the first absorption and the *samādhi* [of those levels] lack initial and sustained application.

Furthermore, it is said that there is perfect enlightenment (samyaksambodhi) by virtue of the accomplishment of the task, not because of the continued existence of its essence, just as with the five faculties of those in training (śaikṣa).
Furthermore, it is said that there is perfect enlightenment because it can uproot and eliminate its opposites, just as one speaks of "correct" speech.
Regarding your question, "What is the meaning of 'right speech' (*samyag-vāc*)?
The answer is:
that which is received as a vow never to be broken is called right speech, as in the tradition of Ghoṣila.
Furthermore, this speech is pure because it is free from the stains of aspiration and grasping through their cessation.
Furthermore, that which is obtained through the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as an eternally virtuous practice is called right speech.
Right speech regarding the precepts is of two kinds:
first, not making it known, as the Sūtra says:
"This person is free from false speech and so forth."
Second, it causes [others] to know, as the Sūtra says:
"This person speaks at the proper time, speaks the truth," and so forth.
As for your question: if there is speech, the path of cultivation would lack certainty.
Why is this? As the Buddha has taught, concentration takes sound as its thorn;
if it were absent, it would not constitute a factor of the path.
Answer:
Because they are factors of the Path (*mārgāṅga*), they are not "thorns," just as, for example, the factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*) is not a thorn when one possesses right awakening.
Furthermore, the "thorn" of sound is not fixed, such as [the sound] of seeing a woman.
The Sūtra says:
"Frequently seeing women is a thorn for the cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya).
However, it is not a thorn for an Arhat, because he has already removed the thorn."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The Great Elephant is said to be in meditative concentration even while walking, standing, and so forth; it is likewise tranquil.

If a practitioner of contemplation correctly reflects upon the teaching of the Dharma, the mind will then be in concentration; it is not the case that concentration is absent simply because there is speech.
The Sautrāntika masters say:
"To simply refrain from the four [unwholesome] words is itself right speech.
As it is said in the world:
Having already departed from [the former state], one acts correctly as it is;
as it is said:
"This horse runs swiftly," or "This person continues well."
Regarding your question as to what the meaning of right action (*samyak-karmānta*) is,
the answer is:
the Sūtra states:
Abstaining from bodily misconduct is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"This bodily action is indivisible, non-flowing, and non-distributing; it is sovereign, without grasping, and capable of producing tranquility—this is called right action."
Furthermore, by contemplating the faults [of killing], one distances oneself from taking life—refraining from it, not practicing it, restraining oneself from it, and taking no pleasure in it;
this is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*). As for your question: "If all factors are right action, why is only one designated as such? [it is because it is the most prominent.]
Answer:

If a distinct name cannot be expressed apart from this [specific] name—as in the case of "dharma-dhātu" or "dharma-āyatana"—and because it is not an object of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and so forth, it cannot be made known to others; thus, it is called "right action" (*samyak-karmānta*).
Because it is the basis upon which all karmas depend, it is like a foundation for karma.
As for your question: "If one speaks of 'right action' as being the absence of doing, then since absence is not an act, how can it constitute karma?"
Answer:
One should know that this karma consists of not performing unwholesome actions and protecting wholesome ones.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
I speak of "doing" and I speak of "not doing.
Furthermore, because it can eliminate both black and white karma, I speak of "not doing";
because it can perform counteractive karma (*pratipakṣa-karman*), it is called "doing."

Furthermore, right action is also called "right action-exclusion" (*samyakkarmānta-vivarjana*). By virtue of this designation, the meanings of both "doing" and "not doing" are established for this term.
It is, for example, like saying one "sees" by means of the eye, yet also saying one "does not see" by means of the eye.
If it were not performed, how could one know that this karma exists?
Answer:
There are many causes and conditions by which this karma can be known.
As the Sūtra states:
"There are three kinds of form (*rūpa*): first, that which is visible and resistant; second, that which is invisible and resistant; and third, that which is invisible and non-resistant.
Furthermore, it speaks of the existence of untainted form (*anāsrava-rūpa*).
Furthermore, it is said that [the fruits of action] arise from the seven types of meritorious benefits.
It is also said that there are ten courses of action (karmapatha) through teaching others.

Moreover, it is said that for a bhikṣu, there exists a dharma not subsumed within the eleven bases (āyatana), namely that which is neither visible nor obstructive; this does not refer to the formless (arūpa).
Furthermore, if this karma did not exist, the Noble Eightfold Path would not be complete.
Why is this? Because when one correctly enters meditative observation, the three types of karma are not being performed.
Objection:
This interpretation is not correct. Why is this so?
Because one has already cultivated the three types of action within skillful means, as the Sūtra says:
"When this person sees thus and knows thus, it is right view; they attain the fulfillment of cultivation, as well as right awakening, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
Question: Previously, right speech, right action, and right livelihood were already purified.
Answer:
This statement is made in reliance upon the precepts of the mundane path of detachment from desire.
Furthermore, the prātimokṣa precepts should also not exist.
Why? Because they exist at the time of reception, but later, when one is in a different state of mind, one should no longer be called a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"This karma is called a dam, for it can obstruct the breaking of precepts;
if it were absent, one would be unable to cease evil."
The Sautrāntikas say:
These proofs are exceedingly numerous;
it is most extraordinary that their meaning is not as [you] claim.
Why is this? Your statement that the existence of a non-agent is known because three colors are mentioned is incorrect.

The masters of meditative practice, such as Maudgalyāyana and Aniruddha, state that there exists a form of the meditative object obtained through the power of concentration; because this form is not the objective domain of the eye-faculty, it is said to be "invisible," and because it does not obstruct space, it is called "unimpeded."
If you say: "If that is so,
what is meant by 'name-and-form' (nāmarūpa)?"—
this constitutes a counter-objection to your own position, as it is equivalent to [the case of] non-action (avijñapti).
As for your statement:
"From the teaching of untainted form (*anāsravarūpa*), we know that there exists no agent"—
this argument is not tenable.
This form is also produced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); because the concentration is untainted (*anāsrava*), the form is likewise untainted.
Furthermore, various masters explain that the form of an Arhat is also untainted, because it is not a basis for the outflows (*āsrava*).
An objection states:
This interpretation is not correct.
As the sutra says:
What are the phenomena associated with outflows (*sāsrava*)?
They refer to all eyes, all forms, and so forth.
Because these forms are not the antidote to outflows, they are said to be "associated with outflows."
If that is so, this form would be either with-outflow (*sāsrava*) or without-outflow (*anāsrava*).
Answer:
If that were so, what problem would there be?
Objection: Because the characteristics (lakṣaṇas) are mutually intermingled.
Response:
If there are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) characteristics, how could they be intermingled?
Furthermore, if the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) were exclusively contaminated, why would the Sūtras specifically distinguish it as such rather than speaking of it in general terms?
The Sūtra says:

"As for 'form associated with existence' (bhava-saṃskṛta-rūpa), it is so called because the mind characterized by grasping (upādāna) firmly conceals its basis; therefore, it is named form associated with existence.
You claim that one knows there is no agent due to the efficacy of the seven merits.
This argument is not correct. The Sautrāntika masters say:

Just as you benefit from the donor’s gift through the merit of the recipient, so too, although the donor’s mind is directed elsewhere, because of the prior intention of giving, the mental continuum is successively refined; by virtue of this refinement, it is able to produce future retributions according to their magnitude. It is based on this continuum that one says the donor’s merit grows.

If you say that because of the superiority and inferiority of another's continuum, as well as its functional application, if this [impression] were to proceed within a different mind-stream, how could it be established?
This interpretation is not correct.
Why? Because it is equal to non-action (anabhisaṃskāra).

If you maintain that there is no unmanifest action (*avijñapti*), how can it be established through the superiority or inferiority of another’s continuum, or by following the causes for its application within another’s continuum?
Question:
Since there is no unmanifest action within that which does not increase the category of merit, how can it be constantly produced?
Answer:
Due to the repeated cultivation of the mental attention associated with morality and concentration as conditions, [the latent tendencies] increase and follow along even within the eye.
Question:
If that is so, what is the meaning of the *Ugra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*?
The sūtra says:

"If a bhikṣu maintains the precepts and practices virtue, and having received the robes, food, and other requisites from a donor, has cultivated the concentration of immeasurable mind (*apramāṇa-citta-samādhi*) and personally realized this concentration while dwelling in the forest—by virtue of this enjoyment, one should know with faith that the merit, goodness, and happiness of the donor increase and flow forth immeasurably."
In this regard, what mental attention (*manasikāra*) is present such that it is known to be a correct principle that the continuity [of the action] becomes increasingly superior?

As for your statement: "If there were no manifest action (*vijñapti*) or unmanifest action (*avijñapti*), how could the path of action (*karmapatha*) be established in the case of another's deed? [This is addressed as follows:]

The Sautrāntikas also maintain this view: because of such an instruction, another person may experience the suffering of being killed or otherwise harmed; thus, the instructor’s subtle continuum undergoes an increase in virtue or non-virtue, and by means of this superior transformation, it can produce future retribution in proportion to its magnitude.
If a person performs an action themselves, and as the deed is accomplished, the continuity of that process becomes increasingly superior, it is termed a "path of action" (*karmapatha*).
This meaning should be understood, for the fruit is designated by the name of its cause.

This is the fruit of bodily and vocal actions; the designation "body" and "speech" is likewise conventional. As with the mental [action], there is no informative intimation (avijñapti) for the body and speech.
A certain Venerable One says:

Based on the appropriation of the aggregates of sentient beings, one incurs the offense of killing through the volition of three moments—namely, "I shall kill for myself," "I am killing," and "I have killed."
This interpretation is also incorrect.
Although these three intentions exist, the karmic path (karmapatha) is not necessarily established. Why is this?
If one has not yet severed the life-faculty of a mother or others, yet gives rise to these three intentions, there is no immediate retribution (ānantarya) for a human being;
however, it is indeed possible for a person who takes their own life or the life of another to incur an offense by means of these three intentions.
Objection: Since [the Buddha] is equally invisible [to all],
why is it that some harbor hatred, jealousy, and slander, while others, without instruction, believe and accept [his teachings], and continue to progress toward excellence?
Answer:
There is no such thing as hatred or envy; rather, it is solely through the movement of the mind that the course of action of bodily karma is accomplished.
If one claims that the practitioner possesses a distinct factor separate from the mind, this is not acceptable to me.
Through the application of the mind, this matter is accomplished.
Because this matter is accomplished, the continuity evolves toward excellence;
this meaning is to be rejoiced in.
Why is this? Because the fruit is established through the continuity of the mind.
As for your statement that the Buddha did not teach that the *dharmāyatana* is formless, thereby implying the existence of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
This point has already been answered: it is like the form that serves as the object of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
As for your statement that if this karma did not exist, the Eightfold Path would not be established, and therefore one must know that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) exists—[this is incorrect].
This point should be clarified; friend, you ought to explain it: for one who has entered into the contemplation of the Truths, how can right speech, right action, and right livelihood exist?
Does this person, while in contemplation, still engage in verbal expression, physical action, and the pursuit of the four requisites, such that these three [factors] exist;
or is it otherwise?
Answer: Not so. Why is this?
While in the state of contemplation, one attains these three kinds of non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
Because of this attainment, after emerging from contemplation, one does not abide in improper speech and the like, but dwells instead in right speech and so forth.
Therefore, because the name of the "fruit" is metaphorically applied to the "cause," it is said that non-informative action (avijñapti) is called "right speech" and so forth.
The Master [Vasubandhu] replies:
Why not maintain this very point here?
If one is currently in meditative observation, having departed from non-informative action (*avijñapti*), one attains such a state of mind and such a basis.
Because of attaining this, when subsequently emerging from observation, one does not abide in wrong speech and so forth, but dwells only in right speech and so forth.
Therefore, the name of the fruit is provisionally applied to the cause; thus, the continuous progression toward excellence is called "right speech" and so forth.
For this reason, the Path consists of eight branches.
Furthermore, the Sthavira school asserts:
"Merely refraining from evil is called the three parts. Why is this?
By the power of the Noble Path, phenomena are determined not to arise; because they rely upon the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), they are called "untainted.
It is not necessarily the case that all phenomena enumerated in every context truly exist, as is the case with the eight worldly dharmas (*aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ*).
That is to say: gain and loss, fame and insignificance, praise and blame, pleasure and pain.
Among these, "loss" is nothing other than the absence of a distinct phenomenon.
Furthermore, other masters say:
The Prātimokṣa precepts constitute three divisions of the path.

Based on the prior method, one forms the intention of faith and acceptance; by virtue of this mental engagement, one is able to restrain body and speech and prevent the commission of evil deeds, which is termed the Prātimokṣa precepts.
If you say that when a person is in a different state of mind, there is no protection, this argument is incorrect;
because of repeated practice, when conditions for violating the precepts arise, the corresponding mental attention immediately follows.
This mental attention (*manasikāra*) is called a "dam. Why?
Because it functions by causing one to remember a prior vow not to commit evil; for this purpose, one must receive the precepts.

Furthermore, if it were as you propose—that there exists a distinct non-informative entity capable of preventing the violation of the precepts—then there would be no such thing as committing an offense through loss of mindfulness; this need not be debated at length.
Whether this is so or not, it must be known with certainty:
within the Eightfold Noble Path, ethical discipline (*śīla*) has three aspects; because it serves as the foundation for the path, it is likened to the earth;
because it is practiced first, it is likened to a king.
Because it can cross over the dense forest of the thorns of birth and death, it is likened to feet;

because it possesses a lovely fragrance, it is like celestial sandalwood leaves; and because it is pure and transmitted through successive stages until reaching nirvāṇa, it is like the analogy of the seven chariots.
Furthermore, other masters state:

This precept exists because it is cited in the sūtras as scriptural evidence; because it is the fruit of the Path; because it serves as the cause for respect, gain, and offerings; because it is not a counteragent for guarding [the senses]; and because it causes one to know what has been attained. Thus, they maintain that this precept exists.
Furthermore, other masters say:
How is it that non-informative matter (avijñapti) is form (rūpa) yet is not experienced as bodily sensation?
Answer:
Non-informative action (avijñapti) belongs to bodily and vocal karma and is subsumed under form (rūpa).
Feeling (vedanā) associated with the mind is subsumed under the mental (nāma).
Furthermore, because non-informative action is bodily karma, it belongs to the body; because feeling is a mental factor (caitta), it belongs to the mind.
Furthermore, non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is both discipline (*śīla*) and form (*rūpa*), and is thus subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Physical sensation, mental sensation, mind, and phenomena are subsumed under the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*).

What is being discussed here is that because this phenomenon is the basis for mental karma, it is given its name by way of metaphorical designation based on the accomplishment [of action] through body and speech.
What is the difference between this dharma and feeling (vedanā)?
Answer:
Feeling is subsumed under the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha), whereas this dharma is subsumed under all the aggregates (skandhas).
Why is this? Because it depends upon continuity.
As for your question: why are things such as being free from beating not described as factors of the path?
Answer:
Because the noble ones in training have not yet attained complete tranquility, it is like a proscribed offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
Because it is not universal, it is like unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*).
Because they are indeterminate, they are like the *pāśupata-aṅga* (the ascetic observances).
Because they serve as provisions, they are like giving and so forth.
What is now being discussed are the clearly defined eight precepts; herein they are called the three *ārya-mārgāṅga* (noble path-factors).
Regarding your question as to how right action and right livelihood differ from the right action and right livelihood among the ten wholesome paths of action:
the answer is that they are [respectively] subject to destruction and removal, and not subject to destruction and removal.
Arising from supramundane right view, the fruit is the outflow-free nectar;
arising from mundane right view, the fruit is the appropriated aggregates with outflows.
That which can produce merit is called the path of action (*karmapatha*); that which can transcend merit is called the factor of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
Regarding your question as to the meaning of "right livelihood" (samyag-ājīva):

the answer is that there are two kinds. First, for laypeople, it consists of abstaining from the five types of trade; second, for monastics, it consists of renouncing the five types of wrong livelihood (mithyā-ājīva).
Furthermore, one seeks the four conditions for the enjoyment of clothing, food, and so forth by relying on reason.
Furthermore, one is content and free from faults, being subsumed under the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa), and guards body and speech.
Furthermore, when one first uses wisdom to distance oneself from the improper requisites of body and mind, this is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
As for your question—why right livelihood is established separately if it is subsumed under the actions of body and speech—it is because [it serves as a specific antidote to wrong livelihood].
Answer:
They are generally included within two [categories], yet they may be understood as established separately due to differences in their specific meanings.

For example, although all aggregates (*skandha*) are generally included within the category of formations (*saṃskāra*), four separate aggregates are established because of differences in their specific meanings.
Furthermore, because their essence consists of two parts, they are like the contemplation of the body; as the Sūtra says:
"Abiding in the contemplation of the body, one contemplates the body.
Furthermore, right livelihood differs from the preceding two factors, just as it is distinct from the categories of afflictions.
As for your question regarding what constitutes diligence (*vīrya*):

the answer is that it consists of acting in various circumstances according to the distinctions of each stage, in order to attain diverse wholesome dharmas, exerting both body and mind without abandoning one's burden.
Furthermore, to extinguish unwholesome dharmas and realize wholesome dharmas by constantly practicing with valor is called diligence (*vīrya*).
Furthermore, to apply physical and mental effort in the practice of what is appropriate and not inverted is called diligence.
Regarding your question as to what its characteristics, functions, conditions, and meanings are:
the answer is that its characteristic is the rousing of body and mind; its function is non-retrogression and non-falling away; and its condition is the arousal of the category of diligence.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"Vigor has courage as its characteristic, non-sinking as its function, the four right efforts as its conditions, and beneficial action as its meaning."
If a person is indolent, their conduct yields no benefit.
Furthermore, it is because of the power of being difficult to conquer:
if a person possesses diligence, they possess the power to be difficult to conquer in the battle against the afflictions (*kleśa*); such a thing does not exist for an idle person.
Furthermore, this practice is able to disperse, eliminate, and relinquish [defilements]; this is the meaning of diligence (*vīrya*).
As for your question: if the cessation of evil were itself wholesome, then there would be no two types of diligence;
if it were not wholesome, then the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) would likewise not be wholesome.
Answer:
The cessation of evil is exclusively a non-entity, whereas the good is not so; therefore, diligence is of two kinds.
Furthermore, the cessation of evil is termed "true goodness," while the remainder constitutes the three types of goodness.
Why is this? Because there are four virtues.

To be free from the stench of broken precepts is called the extinction of evil; for the fragrance of the precepts to arise is called the production of good. This is like the difference between the cessation of heat and the arising of cold.
Regarding your question: if cultivating right effort with a single mind were itself sufficient, then there would be no four right efforts;
if they were cultivated sequentially, then the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment would be incomplete.
Answer:
One can cultivate the four right efforts with a single mind, just as one may simultaneously contemplate the Four Noble Truths with a single mind. Why is this?

By means of this cultivation, unarisen evils do not arise, and arisen evils do not persist; wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen come into being, and those already arisen become firmly established.
Therefore, diligence is one in terms of its essence, but fourfold in terms of its function.
Furthermore, the Vibhajyavādins state:

For a practitioner who maintains the precepts and engages in meditative observation, the four right efforts are cultivated as antidotes to counteract obstacles to concentration; thus, unwholesome states that have already arisen—which can obstruct concentration—are eliminated through diligence.

That which has not yet arisen as broken precepts shall not arise hereafter; that which has not yet arisen as fixed attainment shall arise; and those who already possess pure precepts shall cause them to abide firmly.
For this reason, while diligence is singular, its functional applications are fourfold.
Furthermore, some say that the four right efforts arise in succession, just as one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Why is this?

There is right effort that can only destroy the manifest afflictions of the mind; there is another right effort that can uproot the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); furthermore, there is right effort that can cause unarisen roots [of goodness] to arise; and there is yet another right effort that can make those already arisen firm and stable.
Therefore, the cultivation of the factors of the path is not a scattered cultivation, because there is right effort.
As for your question, "What is right mindfulness?
the answer is:
Not forgetting the objects previously known is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), which is like the thorough grasping of a sign.
As the Sūtra says:
"The mind being alert and the mind being bound, etc., this is called mindfulness."
Regarding your question as to what its characteristics, functions, conditions, and meanings are:

the answer is that taking the subsequent recollection of an object as its characteristic, the non-separation of mind and object as its function, the six recollections as its conditions, and the act of remembering oneself and causing others to remember as its meaning— just as *bodhi* (awakening) is both self-awakening and the causing of others to awaken.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
Mindfulness has the characteristic of mental clarity and purity; it does not forget, and if it should be lost, it manifests again.
Furthermore, because it is able to guard the object of perception and serves as the basis for wisdom (*jñāna*), it is called mindfulness (*smṛti*).

Furthermore, there are four kinds of mindfulness: first, that which follows the grasping of names, phrases, and syllables; second, that which can follow the meanings grasped; third, that which can follow the meanings contemplated; and fourth, that which can follow the thorough penetration of the meanings contemplated.
The present treatise primarily elucidates the fourth point.
You have asked: "If all conditioned phenomena do not abide for even a single moment, how can memory be established? Why is this so?
Regarding the statement, "Because there is no such principle as one seeing and another remembering," the answer is:
If the knower were different [from the rememberer], then memory would not be established, just as when Zhang sees and Wang remembers.
If the continuity of cognitions were different [at each moment], then mindfulness would also be impossible, just as one who sees a cow does not remember a horse and so forth.
Furthermore, if cognition were to exist for only a single moment, mindfulness would also be impossible, because there would be no subsequent cognition.
When these three meanings are present, it is called mindfulness (*smṛti*).

Furthermore, another explanation states: if there is no connection [between the subject and the object], then one person seeing another cannot remember them, just as when a person sees someone else, they do not remember that other person.

If there were a causal relationship, then one person would perceive and another would remember; for example, the cognitions of childhood, youth, adulthood, and old age would arise following one another in succession.
Furthermore, it is like a seed: because they lack such a relationship, a barley seed does not produce a rice sprout.
If cause and effect were related yet distinct, then seeds of grain and the like would produce their sprouts, stalks, nodes, and leaves in successive stages.
However, this cannot be established even in a single moment, because cause and effect would not be established; it would be like a seed that remains eternally one and thus never produces a sprout.
Because they are neither different nor identical, mindfulness is established.

As for your question: if all phenomena are the foundations of mindfulness, then it would follow that the faculty of mindfulness is itself the foundation of mindfulness, which would be inconsistent with the meaning.
Answer:

The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) discussed in this treatise is precisely the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*); however, it is not designated as a faculty by way of its objective sphere (*ālambana*), just as, for example, the faculty of wisdom (*jñānendriya*) is not so designated by way of the measure of its wisdom.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): first, the foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*), which merely gives rise to mindfulness, like a king;

second, the mixed foundation of mindfulness (*sambhinna-smṛtyupasthāna*), wherein any dharma that can assist mindfulness is also called "mindfulness," just as a king’s ministers and assistants may also receive the title of "king."

The three objects of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are also called "mindfulness" because mindfulness arises by taking them as its object, just as one refers to a king’s residence as the "king.
Therefore, the faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya) is itself the foundation of mindfulness; there is no contradiction in their meaning.
Regarding your question: "If mindfulness alone cannot maintain a single dharma, why does the Sūtra speak of one who 'maintains a single [object] through mindfulness'?
The answer is:
Mindfulness is the foremost predominant condition among all forms of protection; therefore, it is said that one "maintains a single [object]," just as, for example, a king is said to be victorious.
As the Sūtra says:
"Mindfulness is the predominant condition for all phenomena, because it provides protection.
Furthermore, since a single moment of mindfulness can protect all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), it is called "single-guarding" (*eka-rakṣā*).
As the Sūtra says:
"This mindfulness operates in all places.
Furthermore, all mindfulness can guard the six sense faculties, just as a gatekeeper guards the gates.
Furthermore, this mindfulness can collect the mind into one-pointedness, just as a person’s hand grips the mouth of a pair of *yantra* tubes.
Furthermore, because it can maintain a single continuity, it is called "one-pointed maintenance" (*ekāgratā*), like protecting an only son.

Furthermore, the six sense faculties are bound to the single pillar of one-pointed mindfulness, remaining undispersed within their respective objects, just as six living beings might be tied together to a single pillar.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"There is mindfulness and single-minded guarding."
Regarding your question as to why one can sometimes remember and at other times cannot:

the answer is that there are three causes and conditions by which mindfulness arises. First is repeated practice; through the repeated practice of body, speech, and mind, things appear as they do in a dream.
Second is the characteristic of recollecting objects through their forward and reverse sequences, whether they appear similar or dissimilar;
third is clarity, whereby mindfulness arises from the purity of the mind, just as one can see the reflection of a face in water contained within a clean vessel.
If one reverses these three conditions, one will not be able to recollect.
Furthermore, being oppressed by the intense suffering at the point of death or at birth causes one to lose their original mindfulness; therefore, one does not remember past lives.
Furthermore, there are six causes and conditions that can give rise to mindfulness.
As the verse says:
"Following and reversing, as well as repeated practice, Being in the same place, and gathering together."
The power of meditative concentration and the power of the cause—these six are the causes of mindfulness.
Regarding "concordant" (anuloma): it is like seeing someone who resembles one's child and thereby remembering one's own son.
Regarding "discordant" (pratiloma): it is like remembering the coldness of former times due to contact with heat.
Regarding "frequent practice": it is like naturally recollecting a matter with which one is well-acquainted.
Regarding "convergence in a single place": it is like a person seeing a mango tree and recollecting its sour taste.
The power of meditative concentration is like a person who has attained the three types of higher knowledge (trividyā) recollecting past lives.
The power of the cause is like a noble one (ārya) or a person of great virtuous conduct recollecting their previous births.
Regarding your question, "What is samādhi?
the answer is:
The Sūtra states that the mind’s abiding in stillness is called samādhi.
Furthermore, the Abhidharma-piṭaka states:
that which can gather the dharmas so they do not disperse is called *samādhi*.
Moreover, this continuity of mind cannot be moved by the evil winds of the afflictions, like a lamp in a sealed room.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of samādhi: namely, the mundane and the supramundane.
The mundane kind can produce mundane karmic results, is dissociated from the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), and is able to suppress the active afflictions (kleśas).

That which is supramundane can cause one to transcend and leave the mundane world; it is associated with the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) and is able to uproot latent afflictions (anuśaya).
What is being discussed in this treatise is supramundane concentration.
Regarding your question as to what its characteristics, functions, conditions, and meanings are:
the answer is that its characteristic is the mind’s stable abiding; its function is the subduing of opposing factors; its condition is reliance upon training the mind.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states:

"Taking the single mind as its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), non-distraction as its function (*vṛtti*), the four dhyānas as its condition (*pratyaya*), and settling the mind to make it upright as its meaning (*artha*), it is like an arrow-maker straightening a shaft."
The world speaks of this as the arrow of samādhi; this refers to an arrow that has been straightened.
When the continuity of the mind is thus straightened, it is called samādhi.
As a verse says:
The heart beats with agitation; it is difficult to guard and difficult to restrain.
The wise man makes it straight and well-adjusted, just as an arrow-maker adjusts the shaft.
Furthermore, one can settle the mind in equanimity, just as a charioteer takes a level road and avoids dangerous, winding paths.

The practitioner of meditation is likewise: because they can place the mind within the gate of the object's characteristics and its modes of activity at a state of equanimity, thereby obstructing the evils of non-equanimity, it is called *samādhi*.
Furthermore, when the disease of the five hindrances has been eliminated, it is called *samādhi*, just as a person who is not ill is said to be healthy.
Regarding your question: "If right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) is indeed concentration, then a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) should have no desire or hatred;
if this were not the case, it would contradict reason. [This is addressed as follows:]...

Answer: That which is to be countered remains present; because one attains the fruit, one infers that one has attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*), just as with the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

Furthermore, because the mind is single-pointedly directed toward concentration—just as a bee, though bound in a foul place, longs for the lotus and is thus known to be constantly in its vicinity—one knows it is always in the state of concentration.
The sage is likewise; although he dwells amidst the dust of desire, his mind delights in tranquility, and thus it is known that he is constantly in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, it is like a person who has attained the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*): although ignorance still remains, their clarity is not lost.

Furthermore, just as the Buddha Bhagavān, although possessing vitarka and vicāra, does not emerge from a distracted mind because he is constantly in meditative concentration (samādhi), so too is the concentration of a Srotāpanna; therefore, it does not contradict reason.
Question:
What is the sequence of the eightfold noble path?
Answer:
Because one is able to contemplate the Noble Truths through the principle of dependent origination, right view is established first.
Next, right intention is established by maintaining an unwavering focus upon the phenomena being contemplated.
Following this, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are established in succession.
Regarding the phenomena under investigation, one establishes diligence (*vīrya*) for the purpose of abandoning what is to be abandoned and attaining what is to be attained.
Next, one establishes right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) so as never to forget or lose what has been abandoned or attained.
Because of this non-forgetfulness through mindfulness, the mind does not waver or scatter toward perceived objects; thus, one subsequently establishes right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Furthermore, if these eight factors arise simultaneously, there would be no sequence; yet, it is not unreasonable to explain them in a sequential order.
If a person wishes to attain nirvana, they must first seek right view, just as one who wishes to travel must possess eyes.
One establishes right awakening by means of the discernment that views reality as it has been perceived;
one subsequently establishes right speech by means of what has been discerned. Why is this so?
If there is speech, it is based upon vitarka and vicāra;
acting in accordance with what one says, one next establishes right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
When these two are pure, one next establishes right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
This person abides in ethical discipline; if they arouse exertion, they next establish diligence.
Because there is diligence, mindfulness is not lost, and they next establish right mindfulness.
Because there is mindfulness, the mind is one-pointed and undistracted, and they next establish right concentration.
Furthermore, the Abhidharma-piṭaka states:
"This practice has wisdom as its root. Why is this so?
The realm of the Four Truths is profound; it cannot be understood without wisdom. Therefore, Right View is established first.
When the mind contacts this realm, Right Resolve is established next.
Through these two factors, one causes oneself to know the Four Truths; subsequently, Right Speech is established.
Based on the first two parts, one initiates practice as described; next, right action (*samyak-karmānta*) is established.
Based on the first two parts, one verbally articulates and physically enacts the realization of the Four Noble Truths; next, right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*) is established.
Exerting oneself with body and mind in order to advance toward the principles of the Truths, one next establishes diligence (*vīrya*).
Through this diligence, the mental application regarding the objects of the Four Truths becomes clear and pure; thus, one next establishes right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
By means of this right mindfulness, the mind and all phenomena remain forever undistracted within the sphere of the Four Noble Truths; subsequently, right concentration is established.
Furthermore, by virtue of right view, the practitioner does not fall into overweening pride (*adhimāna*), for they are able to discern their own attainments as they truly are.
From right awakening, one initiates right speech; this is that which has been personally attained and can be transmitted to others.
By means of this right speech, one is able to establish, refute, and resolve, thereby causing others to believe in one's wisdom.
Because of right action, one would rather sacrifice one's life than commit an unrighteous act; thus, one causes others to believe in the precepts beloved by the noble ones (*āryakānta-śīla*).

Because one seeks and employs the four conditions according to the Dharma and in proper measure, one causes others to believe in the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) of contentment through right livelihood.
Furthermore, by means of right view, right awakening, and right speech, one is able to roar the lion’s roar;
by means of right action and right livelihood, one is able to manifest the meaning of what has been taught.
Through right effort, that which has not yet been attained is brought to attainment, and that which has not yet been extinguished is brought to extinction.

Through the presence of right mindfulness, one does not forget the three characteristics during the states of laxity, excitement, or equanimity; therefore, meditative concentration remains free from hindrance.
Because right concentration eliminates the obstacles to meditative absorption and can induce the virtues of the six supernormal powers, one subsequently attains "liberation through both parts.
Furthermore, the Abhidharma-piṭaka states:
"On account of right view, the faculty of faith, the power of faith, and desire are spoken of."
Why is this? Because through wisdom, faith and aspiration are brought to fulfillment.
Through diligence, one is able to encompass right effort, as well as the faculties, powers, and factors of awakening.

Because of right concentration, it encompasses the basis of psychic power consisting of the mastery over the mind, as well as the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and the factors of enlightenment such as joy, tranquility, equanimity, and concentration.
For this reason, one should know that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are subsumed within the Eightfold Path.
Furthermore, right view and right mindfulness belong to the category of vipaśyanā; because ignorance is extinguished by means of these, their fruit is liberation through wisdom (prajñā-vimukti).
The remaining factors of the path belong to the category of śamatha; because desire is abandoned by means of these, their fruit is liberation of mind (citta-vimukti).
Therefore, it is briefly stated that the Path has two divisions: first, vipaśyanā (insight), and second, śamatha (tranquility).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*). By means of this discipline, one uproots the very foundation of hatred and evil.
Right awakening, right effort, and right concentration—these three constitute the aggregate of concentration; by means of these, the evil root of craving is uprooted.
Right view and right mindfulness—these two constitute the aggregate of wisdom; by means of these, the evil root of ignorance is uprooted.
For this reason, the Path consists of three parts.

Furthermore, there are four types of paths: first, the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), which refers to everything prior to the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), by which that path of non-obstruction arises.

Regarding the second, the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*): because it is precisely capable of removing obstacles as its antidote and because afflictions no longer obstruct, it is called "non-obstruction.

Regarding the third, the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*): because it is liberated from the afflictions that were obstructed by the path of non-obstruction, its initial arising is called "liberation."
Regarding the four superior paths (*viśeṣamārga*): all paths remaining after the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) are termed superior paths.
Question:
Why are these four called "paths"?
Answer:
Because one proceeds by means of this toward nirvāṇa, it is called the "path" (mārga).
If that is so, how can liberation (vimukti) and excellence (viśeṣa) be called the path?
Answer:

It is called the "Path" because it is of the nature of the Path, because it is progressively superior, because it causes one to proceed from the preceding to the succeeding, and because it enables one to reach nirvana without remainder.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of paths: first, the path of suffering with slow knowledge; second, the path of suffering with swift knowledge; third, the path of happiness with slow knowledge; and fourth, the path of happiness with swift knowledge. Regarding the "path of happiness":

This means that because it relies upon the four dhyānas in their complete form, because concentration and wisdom are in equilibrium, and because it is a practice free from effort (*anābhoga*), it is called the "path of bliss.

Conversely, all paths that depart from these conditions are called the "path of suffering," namely those that rely upon the *anāgāmya* dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), or the three formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), because they are incomplete, because concentration and wisdom are unequal, and because they involve effortful practice.

In the future dhyāna, there is wisdom but little concentration; in the three formless absorptions (ārūpya), there is concentration but little wisdom; and in the intermediate dhyāna, because the factors are incomplete, both concentration and wisdom are deficient. For this reason, it is called the "path of suffering."
Regarding these two paths: for one whose faculty of faith is predominant, it is termed "slow progress," while for one whose faculty of wisdom is predominant, it is termed "swift progress.
Thus, this Noble Eightfold Path, when categorized by way of its application and faculties, consists of four modes of progress.
Furthermore, the Noble Path is sometimes described as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
What dharma constitutes enlightenment?
It is designated as enlightenment by means of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

Through three types of persons, three grades of enlightenment are accomplished—namely, the enlightenment of śrāvakas, the enlightenment of pratyekabuddhas, and unsurpassed enlightenment—because they are able to extinguish ignorance so that nothing remains.
This is one's own task already accomplished and no longer to be done; because it is awakened to as it truly is, it is called "awakening" (bodhi).

As for the "aids," they are the thirty-seven factors that follow and accompany the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); therefore, they are called "aids."
The thirty-seven [factors] are spoken of by way of their names, not by way of their essential nature.
The essential nature discussed in this treatise consists of only ten, namely: faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, joy, pliancy, equanimity, ethical discipline, and awakening.
The Abhidharma masters say that there are eleven entities, which is to say that they divide the precepts into two: namely, those of body and speech.
Furthermore, other Abhidharma masters say:
The essence consists of thirteen factors, namely the [ten] bases, desire, and the mind.
Although all dharmas attained through the sūtras assist awakening, these ten alone are preeminent; therefore, they are singled out for mention.

The thirty-seven [factors] refer to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the eightfold noble path, and the seven factors of enlightenment.
Question:
Where are these seven categories of factors conducive to awakening established?
Answer:
There are four stages in total: first, the stage of initial practice; second, the stage of penetration; third, the stage of seeing; and fourth, the stage of cultivation.
Question: What is their sequence?
Answer:

This practitioner of meditation has already established themselves in ethical discipline and is capable of discerning the faults of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the merits of nirvāṇa. Apart from the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, there is no other expedient means by which one can thoroughly understand these faults and merits. In order to collect the mind—which is scattered across many objects—and cause it to abide in a single point; in order to generate antidotes to subdue the four inversions (*viparyāsa*); and in order to cause the mind to enter the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths according to reality, one first contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Having distinguished through the four foundations of mindfulness those phenomena that are to be adopted and those to be abandoned—in order to adopt the wholesome and abandon the unwholesome—one next practices the right efforts (*samyak-pradhāna*).

Because the right efforts are accomplished by means of the four foundations of mindfulness, and because the hindrances of affliction have been purified and the auxiliary factors established through the observation of the right efforts, so that the mind dwells according to one’s will, one next establishes the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
By virtue of this power of concentration (*samādhi*), the mind gains supremacy regarding objects that are free from doubt.
By virtue of this faith (*śraddhā*), the mind gains supremacy regarding non-laziness (*apramāda*).

The virtuous mind obtained through this diligence (*vīrya*) is assisted and unimpeded, whereby the mind gains supremacy regarding objects that are not forgotten; by virtue of this mindfulness (*smṛti*), the mind is gathered into a single object, whereby the mind gains supremacy regarding non-distraction (*avikṣepa*).

Because of this concentration, the mind has predominance in observing the object as it truly is; because of this predominance in its essential nature, the mind has predominance in the stage of non-retrogression; and because of non-retrogression, the mind has predominance in the stage of penetration. Therefore, the five faculties are established next.

Because these five faculties have increased to the highest degree, because inferior afflictions cannot destroy them, because other worldly dharmas cannot surpass them, because they serve as the immediate conditions for the outflow-free mind, and because one does not fall back from the stage of a noble one—for these reasons, the five powers are established next.

Having already perceived the gains and losses of both sides, having attained the true path, having attained the resolute mind, having attained the eye, and having attained the feet, one emerges into supramundane practice by means of the five powers; therefore, the Noble Eightfold Path is established next.

Once the delusions regarding the truths have been shattered by means of the Eightfold Noble Path, one attains proximity to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); therefore, this path is further designated as the Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
For this reason, thirty-seven factors are established in this sequential order.

The contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness is the stage of initial practice, which is the factor conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); the four right efforts are called the stage of patience (*kṣānti*); the four bases of psychic power are called the stage of designation (*nāmabhūmi*); the five faculties are called the stage of characteristics (*lakṣaṇabhūmi*); and the five powers are called the stage of the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharmabhūmi*). These four stages are collectively termed the stage of definitive resolution (*niścayabhūmi*).

The Eightfold Noble Path is termed the stage of vision (darśana-bhūmi); the Seven Factors of Enlightenment are termed the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-bhūmi); and the Knowledge of Destruction (kṣaya-jñāna) and the Knowledge of Non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) are termed the ultimate stage (niṣṭhā-bhūmi). As these are effects rather than causes, they are not established as the Path.
Furthermore, this path is also called the "Brahma-wheel" (*brahmacakra*),
because it is turned by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and his disciples.
This Noble Path possesses six characteristics that are analogous to a wheel.
First is swift movement, which refers to either one mind, twelve minds, or fifteen minds that pervade the four truths of the three realms; therefore, it is called "swift."
Second, abandoning this and reaching that, meaning abandoning the mundane and reaching the supramundane, and so forth.
Third, because of moving upward and downward, meaning being sometimes in the *dharmakṣānti* (patience regarding the dharma) and sometimes in the *anvayakṣānti* (subsequent patience), and so forth.
Fourth, it proceeds from one to another; that is, the understanding transmitted sequentially from teacher to teacher reaches the understanding of the disciple’s lineage.
Fifth, because they resemble the hub, spokes, and rim [of a wheel]:
the three divisions of the precepts constitute the hub; right view, right awakening, right diligence, and right mindfulness constitute the spokes; and right concentration constitutes the rim.
The wheel of the six noble kings can subdue those not yet subdued and protect those already subdued.

Because it can subdue by means of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and protect by means of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is for this reason called the Brahma-wheel (*brahmacakra*).
Furthermore, regarding these eight noble factors, right view consists of five parts;
morality consists of six kinds, namely the three types of informative and non-informative action;
and diligence consists of nine parts.
Right mindfulness has eight factors;
right concentration likewise has eight factors.

If this Noble Path is explained extensively, it consists of thirty-seven factors; if explained intermediately, it consists of eight factors; if explained concisely, it consists of either three factors or two factors.
The verse says: If a person seeks nirvana— cessation, tranquility, and sublime detachment—
they should constantly practice diligence and listen to, contemplate, and cultivate the Four Noble Truths.
